description:
The Engineers is a two-member team of Software Engineering students from Istanbul Health and Technology University (ISTUN), participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

We are taking on the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” With a shared passion for technology, software development, and space exploration, we aim to develop an innovative solution that helps astronauts monitor and evaluate their health during long-duration space missions.
summary: Orbit Health Check is a web dashboard that helps astronauts assess their own health when a doctor is far away. The crew enters heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep and mood, and the tool shows a green, yellow or red status with a plain-language reason, the related NASA Human Research Program hazard, and simple general actions. It also shows trends over time, a clickable body map, and how communication delays on the Moon or Mars change the advice. It runs in any browser using synthetic sample data only, and it is for demonstration, not a medical diagnosis.
details:
Orbit Health Check is a browser-based dashboard that helps astronauts assess their own health when a doctor is far away. It was built for the challenge "Health Monitoring Software".

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The astronaut enters five indicators: heart rate (bpm), systolic blood pressure (mmHg), blood sugar (mg/dL), daily sleep (hours) and a 1-5 mood rating. Each value gets a green, yellow or red status shown with an icon and text, so it never relies on color alone, plus an overall status. A "Why this result?" panel shows which illustrative range was used. For every indicator the tool explains how it can be measured in space, why it matters, how spaceflight hazards can affect it, when to alert the crew or ground flight surgeons, and which simple general actions can help. Each indicator carries a tag for the most related NASA Human Research Program hazard. Simple rule-based trend alerts warn when a value moves in a worrying direction over the last readings. A time-series chart shows 14 days of synthetic history plus the user's own entries.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions, such as a Mars transit with about 20 minutes of one-way communication delay (approximate), astronauts must spot health changes themselves. The tool gives a quick, clear, plain-language picture and tells the crew what to do first, while messaging the ground team in parallel. It also creates a one-page printable summary and a CSV file that could be shared with a flight surgeon. It could help crews notice problems earlier and make health information easier to understand for people who are not medical experts.

CREATIVITY

A clickable human body map shows the function, current status and spaceflight effects for the brain, heart, bones and immune system. An environment selector (ISS, Moon base, Mars transit) changes the guidance wording and shows the approximate communication delay. Demo scenarios, an in-page reminder banner and a daily check-in streak with badges make routine health checks more engaging.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks, external libraries, backend, database or API keys. Charts and the body figure are drawn with inline SVG. Data is saved in the browser with localStorage. The site is static, hosted on Vercel, and the code is on GitHub. No special hardware is needed; it runs in a browser on a laptop or phone. We used the AI assistant Claude to help write code and text (see the AI use section), and we reviewed and tested the result.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Safety: the tool is for demonstration and is not a medical diagnosis, and all thresholds are illustrative general reference ranges chosen by our team, not official clinical or NASA thresholds. Honesty: all sample data is synthetic, and we do not invent NASA thresholds or citations. Privacy: no personal data is collected, and everything stays in the user's browser. Accessibility: keyboard navigation, visible focus, ARIA labels and high contrast. Usability: a responsive layout and simple language for people who are not medical experts. Relevance: the explanations are based on the five hazards of human spaceflight from the NASA Human Research Program, summarized in our own words.
